When the district announced the new bell schedule in August, administrators described it as a modest adjustment: a late start on Wednesdays, a few minutes trimmed from each period, and one longer block in the middle of the day. Eight weeks in, students say the change has rearranged almost everything else about their school lives.

Lunch is the most visible casualty. The cafeteria was designed for three waves of roughly 400 students; the new schedule compresses those waves into two. On a typical Thursday, the line for the hot entrée stretches past the library doors by 11:42, and the last students in line are often seated with fewer than ten minutes left.

What changed, and when

The school board approved the revised schedule on June 12 after a 4–3 vote. Supporters pointed to research linking later start times to better attendance. Opponents, including two members who represent the district’s eastern attendance zone, warned that the compressed lunch periods would create supervision and capacity problems that the plan did not address.

  1. June 12

    Board approves new schedule

    The vote is 4–3. Two dissenting members ask for a cafeteria capacity study that is never scheduled.

  2. Aug. 19

    Families notified by email

    The message goes out four working days before classes begin and does not mention the lunch changes.

  3. Sept. 3

    First Wednesday late start

    Buses arrive on a staggered plan; 212 students are marked tardy in the first week.

  4. Sept. 24

    Student council petition

    Signed by 614 students, the petition asks for a third lunch wave.

  5. Oct. 8

    Principal meets council

    Administrators agree to “review options” but commit to no changes before January.

  6. Fall 2027

    Cafeteria renovation planned

    The district’s long-range facilities plan, not yet funded, would add 120 seats.

Nutrition staff say the two-wave model has also changed what students eat. Food service director Karen Alvarado said sales of cold packaged items rose 38 percent between September and October, while hot entrée sales fell by roughly a fifth. “When the line is long, kids grab what they can carry,” she said.

How we reported this

Reporters reviewed board minutes from June 12 and August 21, interviewed eleven students, four teachers and two administrators, and requested cafeteria sales data under the state public records law. The district provided figures covering September 3 through October 17.

11:38 a.m. The doors open

Seniors with first-wave lunch cross the quad together; the cafeteria holds the line to the library.

11:51 a.m. Nine minutes left

Students who joined the line at 11:42 sit down with a tray and a countdown. Several leave half their food behind.

12:03 p.m. Back to class

The second wave is already forming outside. The first wave walks against them to fourth period.

The district has said it will publish the results of a survey of families in November. Until then, students say, they will keep eating on the move.
